The exit is a convenient culprit, but the slide started before it. Copper has dropped every week since mid-October, and Goldman Sachs called the correction a matter of positioning in AI-linked stocks, not a sign that fundamentals have loosened. Three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange was down 0.5% at $13,519 a metric ton as of 1000 GMT, after touching $13,456, its weakest since July 17. As the Nvidia news broke on Thursday, Panmure Liberum analyst Tom Price put it bluntly: “Every time AI takes a hit, copper demand and prices come under pressure too.” He also pointed to stubborn US inflation and the prospect of Federal Reserve rate hikes. Nvidia said Huang resigned Thursday as president, CEO and director, effective immediately. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress is interim CEO while keeping her finance job, and Harvey Jones becomes the board’s first chair. Shares closed 4.3% lower Thursday and fell about 2% more on Friday . Bloomberg reported that results are due Nov. 17, with Kress promising an all-hands meeting the next day. Huang has also agreed to testify before Congress by Thanksgiving, House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said, adding that “he has some very serious questions to answer.” The route from a boardroom crisis to the copper market runs through financing. UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri said Nvidia has become a key source of funds for neoclouds and AI developers, and expects a pause in its appetite for those deals even if a new CEO holds the same course. JPMorgan analysts said they do not assume existing commitments change, but new deals could take longer or cost more. Goldman said copper positioning could stay subdued if equity markets start pricing an earlier slowdown in AI spending, even while data center construction continues. The gap matters because much of the money is not going into buildings. Mining.com’s Frédéric Tomesco and Colin McClelland flagged the builders’ budgets on Thursday. Microsoft CFO Amy Hood told investors Oct. 28 that calendar-year capital spending would reach about $170 billion , and about three-quarters of its latest quarterly spending went to short-lived assets such as chips. Alphabet held its 2026 forecast at $195 billion to $205 billion. S&P Global sees copper demand reaching 42 million metric tons by 2040, up 50%, with AI and defense each roughly tripling and adding about 4 million tons between them. Developers are also building their own power. Oilprice.com contributors Leonard Hyman and William Tilles wrote this week that published estimates point to 30 to 50 gigawatts of on-site generation at data centers within five years, mostly gas turbines. Physical buyers in China are not behaving like a market braced for weaker demand. The Yangshan copper premium, a gauge of China’s appetite for imports, hit a record $285 a ton on Friday, and copper stocks in Shanghai Futures Exchange warehouses fell 18.3% this week to 27,642 tons, the lowest since Dec. 23, Reuters reported. The gold-silver ratio is the oldest relative-value measure in precious metals: it simply divides the gold price by the silver price. For most of monetary history the ratio was fixed near 15:1; in the modern free-market era it has ranged widely — from below 20 to above 100 — moving as the two metals respond differently to industrial cycles and investment flows. Traders watch the ratio as a gauge of how the two metals are priced relative to each other and to their own history. A rising ratio means gold is outperforming silver; a falling ratio means silver is gaining ground. The spot price is the market price for one troy ounce of silver for immediate delivery, quoted in U.S. dollars. A troy ounce is 31.1034768 grams — about 10% heavier than the avoirdupois ounce used for groceries. Physical silver products trade at a premium above spot that covers fabrication and distribution — and because silver is far less valuable per gram than gold, the premium is proportionally larger: minting a one-ounce silver coin costs nearly as much as minting a gold one, but represents a much bigger share of the metal’s value. The spot price is for silver delivered now; a futures price is for silver delivered on a set date in the future, traded on exchanges such as COMEX. The two normally differ by the cost of carrying silver to that date — storage, insurance and interest — which is why futures usually trade slightly above spot ( contango ). When futures trade below spot ( backwardation ), it signals unusually strong demand for immediate physical delivery. summary: It was driven by energy inflation, which surged above 20% in October.
body: Inflation in the euro area jumped to a three-year high of 4% in October, a flash estimate showed on Wednesday. The reading is in line with the expectations of economists polled by Reuters and was up from 3.8% in September . Officials said the increase was largely due to surging energy costs, with energy inflation rising to 20.8% from 18.9% in September. Europe, a net energy importer, is vulnerable to external energy shocks and has seen prices rise steadily since the start of the Iran war. October marked the first time inflation in the euro zone has hit or exceeded the 4% threshold since Sept. 2023's reading of 4.3%. Inflation also varied across the 21 euro zone economies, with Lithuania recording the hottest inflation rate of 6.1% while Malta's was the lowest at 2.3%. All euro zone countries saw inflation hold above the European Central Bank's 2% target. The euro was up 0.6% against the U.S. dollar on Wednesday morning, although the greenback fell against a basket of major currencies as counting continued in the U.S. midterm elections, while the yield on the 10-year German bund — broadly seen as a benchmark for euro zone bonds — was marginally higher. Policymakers said underlying inflation and wages were broadly stable, despite inflation sitting at a three-year high. The European Central Bank kept its key interest rate at 2.5% last month, following a hike of 25 basis points in September. Shortly before Wednesday's inflation print, markets were pricing in a 71.8% chance of a hike at the ECB's final meeting of the year in December. Following the data release, markets were pricing in more than a 72% chance of rates rising. Robert Mertens, global capital markets senior analyst at Validus Risk Management, cautioned that "ongoing turmoil in the French bond market is placing constraints on ECB policy" and the bank's capacity to get inflation under control. "Should we see an easing in French political unrest, the ECB could potentially pursue a more aggressive hiking path," he said. "If the ECB can deploy more aggressive tightening relative to the Federal Reserve, we would see increased Euro support and upside versus the Dollar."

Fourth-quarter oil supply to exceed demand by 1.7mn bpd; IEA had previously forecast a fourth-quarter supply deficit; IEA also gives more details of emergency oil stock release The world oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of this year, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Friday, as Middle East exports recover faster than global oil demand despite continued attacks on shipping. The agency also gave more details of remaining volumes to come from a record release of oil from its members' emergency reserves pledged in March, saying 71mn barrels would be made available by the end of February including 15mn barrels of diesel to ease market tightness. Oil supply will average 105mn barrels per day in the fourth quarter, the Paris-based agency, which advises industrialised countries, said in a monthly report, 1.7mn bpd higher than forecast demand. The IEA had previously forecast a fourth-quarter supply deficit. "The oil market is showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran," the agency said in the report. Oil prices reversed earlier gains after the IEA report was released at 0900 GMT. Brent crude was last down 0.1% at $95.71 a barrel. The report follows signs that Gulf oil producers are recovering exports disrupted since the start of the war in late February by using workarounds such as so-called dark crossings through the Strait of Hormuz, where tankers switch off tracking signals to evade attack. The Opec+ group, which includes the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies such as Russia, pumped 41.23mn bpd of crude in October, Opec said on Wednesday, up about 2.04mn bpd from September and 97% of the pre-war February volume. Other analysts have also forecast a return to excess supply, despite the lack of a resolution to the Iran war and continuing tanker attacks in the Gulf. JPMorgan last week forecast a global surplus of 1.4mn bpd in October. High oil prices have also curbed demand this year, helping tip the balance into a surplus. World oil demand is forecast to fall by 2.7mn bpd in 2026 to 102.3mn bpd before rebounding by 2mn bpd in 2027, the IEA said, little changed from its previous forecasts. As well as rising output from Opec+, the IEA flagged supply rising from outside the group. Production from the United States, Canada, Brazil, Argentina and Guyana will rise by 1.6mn bpd this year, the IEA said. In 2027, global supply is projected to rise by 6.6mn bpd to 108.1mn bpd, led by a further recovery in Gulf output. Still, the 2027 supply growth forecast is down 1.1mn bpd from last month's report, and the lower outlook partly reflects a downward revision from Iran, the IEA said. Iran is subject to a US blockade that has curbed its oil exports. For 2027, the IEA sees the supply surplus at about 3.8mn bpd, slightly down from a 3.94mn bpd surplus last month.

body: Felicity Bradstock is a writer and journalist based in Mexico City. She writes for energy websites and covers several other industries, as well as writing… Several oil and gas companies in the United States have benefited from increased trade following the war in Iran that began in February, and from subsequent restrictions on international energy trade. Many countries have been forced to turn to alternative suppliers due to restrictions on movement through the Strait of Hormuz, the critical waterway connecting the Persian Gulf to the Arabian Sea, a shift that has allowed U.S. oil majors to help fill the gap. The Strait of Hormuz has faced severe, ongoing restrictions and a functional blockade since late February 2026, following attacks on Iran by the United States and Israel, which led Tehran to respond by limiting movement through the waterway. Prior to the trade restrictions, the Strait of Hormuz was used to transport around one-fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG). In 2025, roughly 20 million barrels of oil and oil products passed through the waterway every day, equivalent to almost $600 billion in energy trade per year, according to estimates from the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA). As Iran continues to impose trade restrictions, several countries have been forced to halt energy exports , particularly in the Persian Gulf, resulting in a severe negative impact on certain economies. Uncertainties about how and when the Strait of Hormuz may reopen, and what energy trade might look like going forward, have led many countries around the globe to rapidly seek new fuel suppliers. The recent trade restrictions have exposed vulnerabilities in global energy trade and demonstrated the importance of diversification – both in energy exports and in expanding production beyond fossil fuels to renewable alternatives. A recent New York Times analysis suggests (conservatively) that U.S. oil firms have earned over $130 billion in profit this year, owing to higher fuel prices and increased demand for certain products. This assessment is based on the performance of over 50 major U.S. oil and gas companies, mainly producers and refiners, between April and September. By contrast, these companies earned less than $47 billion between them in the same period last year. Some companies are seeing higher profits than others, particularly those in the U.S. refining industry. Several Middle Eastern and Russian refining facilities have been damaged in recent years due to ongoing conflicts, threatening the world’s refining capacity and allowing U.S. oil companies to step in to fill the gap. U.S. companies can continue to operate safely and securely while several Middle Eastern refining companies must operate under dangerous conditions due to the ongoing conflict. In addition, U.S. oil and gas companies are largely sheltered from the high costs of shipping, as much of the oil they process is transported via pipeline. The largest U.S. oil and gas companies, Exxon Mobil and Chevron, have been two of the firms to profit most from the war, reporting sky-high third-quarter earnings in October. Exxon’s third-quarter profit more than doubled, while Chevron’s nearly tripled. body: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ( TSM ) makes the chips for Nvidia ( NVDA ) and the rivals investors bought after Nvidia announced Jensen Huang’s resignation on Nov. 12. That day Nvidia fell , while AMD ( AMD ) and Broadcom ( AVGO ) rose. Someone building chips to take on Nvidia has a different favorite. On the 20VC podcast , Harry Stebbings asked Walter Goodwin, founder and CEO of chip startup Fractile, which of his suppliers he’d invest in. Goodwin picked TSMC: “It is cheap at the price. I would buy that stock every day of the week.” Goodwin’s reason is practical. New chip entrants face “a real challenge” in “accessing, for instance, TSMC capacity, HBM capacity,” he said. Of the custom AI chips he listed, including OpenAI’s, he added: “All of those are rumored to be using Broadcom, for instance. Same or very similar TSMC process nodes, same HBM technology.” So if chip orders shift from Nvidia to AMD or Broadcom-built designs, TSMC still makes the chips. TSMC’s October revenue rose 59.7% from a year earlier to a record NT$586.9 billion (about US$17.8 billion), and analysts expect revenue to keep climbing: Consensus takes revenue from $120.6 billion in 2025 to $294.5 billion in 2028, 2.44 times as much. Huang’s exit doesn’t change how many wafers an AI chip needs, whoever designs it. Gross margin reached 66.4% in the third quarter of 2026 , well above management’s long-term target of 56% or higher. TSMC has credited high utilization and cost improvements for the gains. TSMC’s largest customer, which it doesn’t name, was 19% of 2025 revenue , up from 12% in 2024, and Nvidia is widely reported to be that customer. If Nvidia ordered more than it can sell, TSMC would feel it in future orders. Share shifts between chip designers matter less to TSMC than to the designers. The bigger risk is an AI spending slowdown, which would likely hit several of its big customers together. Nvidia reports on Nov. 17, and its outlook is the next read on those orders.
